title: Orchitis
subject: Pathology
summary: Acute inflammation of the testis, usually bacterial or viral, presenting with pain, swelling and systemic signs. Diagnosis relies on history, exam and basic labs; treatment is prompt antibiotics and supportive care.

sections.p: Orchitis is inflammation of the testis, often with epididymal involvement. It is diagnosed clinically by pain, swelling, erythema and systemic features, confirmed by basic labs and imaging when available.

t.b: Rule out neutrophilia indicating bacterial infection; leukocytosis supports acute inflammation
Detect pyuria or haematuria suggesting urinary source
Differentiate abscess, torsion or tumour; shows increased echogenicity and hyperemia

sections.p: Severity is graded by pain intensity, systemic signs and organ dysfunction. Mild cases respond to oral antibiotics; severe cases may need IV therapy and surgical drainage.
b: Mild: localized pain, low fever, no systemic toxicity
Moderate: high fever, significant swelling, possible abscess
Severe: septic shock, testicular necrosis, potential loss of fertility

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, the leading causes are bacterial epididymo‑orchitis and viral mumps orchitis. Other important causes include TB, schistosomiasis, and HIV‑related opportunistic infections.
b: Enteric gram‑negative bacilli (E. coli) from urinary tract
Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae in children
Schistosoma haematobium eggs causing granulomatous inflammation

t.b: Identify bacterial pathogen; guides antibiotic choice
Positive IgM confirms viral orchitis
Suggests TB involvement if positive

sections.p: Patients report sudden, severe testicular pain, often with swelling and erythema. Systemic symptoms like fever, chills, and nausea are common. In children, pain may be less localized.
b: Pain starts abruptly, may radiate to groin
Redness and warmth over the testis

t.b: Look for tenderness, guarding, and testicular enlargement; check for cremasteric reflex
Ask about recent infections, sexual activity, trauma, or vaccination status

sections.p: Basic investigations are essential; advanced imaging is used when available. Results guide treatment and rule out mimics.

t.b: Detects pyuria or haematuria; positive suggests urinary source
Differentiates abscess, torsion, tumour; shows increased vascularity in orchitis
Positive confirms viral orchitis

sections.p: Urgent red flags include sudden testicular loss, severe pain unrelieved by analgesia, high fever, or signs of sepsis. Complications may be abscess, infertility, or testicular necrosis.

t.b: Monitor temperature, heart rate, blood pressure; abnormal values indicate systemic involvement
Detect abscess formation or evolving necrosis

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause with appropriate antibiotics, provide analgesia, and monitor for complications. Supportive care includes scrotal elevation and rest.
b: Empiric antibiotics: fluoroquinolone + ceftriaxone (or amoxicillin‑clavulanate if STI suspected)

t.b: Cover gram‑negative urinary pathogens; avoid aminoglycosides due to nephrotoxicity
NSAIDs for pain; avoid NSAIDs if renal impairment suspected
Elevate testis to reduce edema

sections.p: Patients should be reassessed in 48–72 hours; repeat ultrasound if pain persists. Prevention focuses on vaccination against mumps and safe sexual practices.

t.b: Mumps vaccine reduces incidence of viral orchitis
Prevents sexually transmitted epididymo‑orchitis

sections.p: Differential includes testicular torsion, epididymitis alone, hernia, tumour, and trauma.
b: Testicular torsion – sudden, severe pain, absent cremasteric reflex

t.b: Absent in torsion, present in orchitis

sections.p: Normal ultrasound may miss early abscess; leukocytosis can be absent in early viral cases; urine dipstick may be negative if infection is purely testicular.
b: Early abscess – ultrasound may appear normal

t.b: If clinical suspicion remains high

whenToSeekHelp: Severe pain not relieved by analgesia

faq.q: Can orchitis happen in both testes?
faq.a: Yes, but unilateral involvement is more common; bilateral disease may suggest systemic infection or mumps.
Yes, routine mumps vaccination prevents most cases.
Most bacterial cases respond, but viral orchitis requires supportive care; complications may persist.

exam: A 16‑year‑old presents with sudden left testicular pain and fever. What is the first step in management? — Assess for torsion, check cremasteric reflex, then start empiric antibiotics if reflex present.
A 30‑year‑old man with epididymo‑orchitis has persistent pain after 48 hours of antibiotics. What is the next investigation? — Repeat scrotal ultrasound to look for abscess.
Why is a fluoroquinolone chosen for bacterial orchitis in a low‑resource setting? — It covers E. coli and is orally available; alternatives may be unavailable or more toxic.
What red flag would prompt immediate surgical exploration? — Sudden testicular loss or absent cremasteric reflex.
How does mumps orchitis differ clinically from bacterial orchitis? — Mumps causes bilateral pain, low fever, and is confirmed by IgM serology.
What is the main complication of untreated orchitis? — Testicular abscess or necrosis leading to infertility.
